currentKeyText: Take calcium with food and vitamin D on an empty stomach.
newKeyText: Take calcium and vitamin D together at the same time.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Calcium and vitamin D can be taken together; no separation is needed.
• Vitamin D actually enhances calcium absorption, and calcium carbonate is best absorbed with food; vitamin D is fat-soluble and also absorbs best with a meal (BHOF 2022). Separate both from alendronate, which must be taken fasting.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Take calcium in the morning and vitamin D at night**: No timing benefit to splitting them.
• **Take calcium with food and vitamin D on an empty stomach**: Vitamin D is better absorbed with food, not on an empty stomach.
• **Take calcium and vitamin D with a high-fiber meal**: High-fiber meals can reduce calcium absorption.
## Key takeaway
Take calcium (with food) and vitamin D together, at a different time from alendronate.
(Guideline: BHOF 2022 osteoporosis guideline; NIH ODS calcium/vitamin D)

## Why this answer is correct
Liraglutide (GLP-1 RA) best meets her goals of weight loss and glucose lowering.
• ADA SOC 2026 recommends a GLP-1 RA (or dual GIP/GLP-1 RA) when weight management is a goal; these have high glucose-lowering and weight-loss efficacy with low hypoglycemia risk.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add glimepiride 4 mg daily**: Sulfonylureas cause weight gain and hypoglycemia.
• **Start canagliflozin 100 mg daily**: SGLT2 inhibitors cause only modest weight loss and are prioritized for HF/CKD, not stated here.
• **Add pioglitazone 15 mg daily**: Pioglitazone causes weight gain.
## Key takeaway
With obesity as a priority, add a GLP-1 RA to metformin.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 9 and 8)

## Why this answer is correct
The HbA1c of 9.5% is the finding that needs follow-up.
• An A1c of 9.5% is well above the usual <7% goal and warrants treatment intensification (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Stable weight**: Stable weight is not concerning.
• **No renal impairment**: Normal renal function is reassuring.
• **Current metformin use**: Metformin use is appropriate and should continue.
## Key takeaway
An A1c far above goal signals the need to intensify therapy.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 6 and 9)

## Why this answer is correct
Counsel her to report unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness.
• Statin-associated muscle symptoms are the most common reason for statin discontinuation, and rare rhabdomyolysis must be recognized early (ACC/AHA 2018).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Avoid grapefruit juice**: Grapefruit interacts meaningfully only in large amounts with atorvastatin (major concern is simvastatin/lovastatin).
• **Take atorvastatin with food**: Atorvastatin can be taken without regard to food.
• **Report any new onset of diabetes symptoms**: New-onset diabetes risk is small and not the primary counseling point.
## Key takeaway
Muscle symptoms are the key statin counseling point.
(Guideline: ACC/AHA 2018 cholesterol guideline; atorvastatin labeling)

currentKeyText: Contact the prescriber for a BUD.
newKeyText: Assign a BUD based on the stability of the ingredients.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
The pharmacist assigns the BUD based on the preparation's stability data.
• Under USP <795>, the compounder assigns the beyond-use date using ingredient stability and USP default limits; prescribers do not supply BUDs.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Contact the prescriber for a BUD**: The prescriber is not responsible for a BUD.
• **Prepare the cream without a BUD**: Every compounded preparation must be labeled with a BUD.
• **Inform the patient that the cream can be used indefinitely**: Compounded preparations cannot be used indefinitely.
## Key takeaway
The compounding pharmacist assigns the BUD per USP <795>.
(Guideline: USP <795> Nonsterile Compounding (2023))

currentKeyText: Increase the dose of glipizide to improve glycemic control.
newKeyText: Add a GLP-1 receptor agonist to his regimen.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist lowers glucose and addresses his weight gain.
• ADA SOC 2026 favors a GLP-1 RA when weight is a concern; it gives strong A1c lowering without adding hypoglycemia (reduce the sulfonylurea if needed).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase the dose of glipizide to improve glycemic control**: Raising glipizide worsens weight gain and hypoglycemia risk.
• **Switch from metformin to insulin therapy**: Metformin should continue, and insulin adds weight.
• **Continue current medications without changes**: A1c 8.5% requires intensification.
## Key takeaway
For weight gain on a sulfonylurea, add a GLP-1 RA.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026, Sec. 9)

## Why this answer is correct
A complete blood count is most important to assess the bruising and nosebleeds.
• New bleeding signs on apixaban call for a CBC to check hemoglobin/hematocrit and platelets for occult blood loss (2023 AF guideline bleeding evaluation).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Renal function**: Renal function should be monitored periodically but does not assess bleeding.
• **Liver function**: Liver function is not the immediate concern.
• **International normalized ratio (INR)**: INR does not reflect apixaban effect.
## Key takeaway
Bleeding on a DOAC: check a CBC, not an INR.
(Guideline: Apixaban labeling; 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline)

currentKeyText: Check for potential drug interactions with oral contraceptives.
newKeyText: Contact the prescriber to discuss alternative therapies.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Contact the prescriber, because combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in migraine with aura.
• US MEC 2024 rates combined estrogen-containing contraceptives category 4 (unacceptable risk) in migraine with aura because of ischemic stroke risk; a progestin-only or nonhormonal method is needed.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Counsel the patient on the proper use of sumatriptan / Advise the patient to take sumatriptan at the onset of her migraine**: Counseling on sumatriptan use ignores the contraindicated contraceptive.
• **Check for potential drug interactions with oral contraceptives**: There is no clinically significant sumatriptan-OC interaction.
## Key takeaway
Migraine with aura plus combined OC: contact the prescriber about switching contraception.
(Guideline: CDC US MEC 2024 (migraine with aura: CHC category 4))

## Why this answer is correct
Dapagliflozin is the most appropriate option for a patient with diabetes and CKD.
• KDIGO 2022 and ADA SOC 2026 recommend an SGLT2 inhibitor for T2D with eGFR at least 20 mL/min for kidney and CV protection; metformin can also continue at eGFR 45.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Glyburide**: Glyburide carries high hypoglycemia risk in CKD and should be avoided.
• **Insulin detemir**: Insulin is not needed.
• **Sitagliptin**: Sitagliptin requires dose reduction at eGFR 30-45 and lacks kidney benefit.
## Key takeaway
In T2D with CKD, choose an SGLT2 inhibitor.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 9/11; KDIGO 2022 diabetes in CKD)

## Why this answer is correct
The potassium of 3.2 mEq/L warrants a therapy change.
• Hypokalemia from loop diuretics increases arrhythmia risk in heart failure; replace potassium or add a potassium-sparing agent such as an MRA if appropriate (ACC/AHA/HFSA 2022).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Serum creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL**: SCr 2.5 reflects her known CKD and is not the acute problem here.
• **Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) of 30 mg/dL**: BUN 30 is consistent with CKD/diuresis.
• **Sodium level of 138 mEq/L**: Sodium 138 is normal.
## Key takeaway
Correct hypokalemia in HF patients on loop diuretics.
(Guideline: ACC/AHA/HFSA 2022 heart failure guideline)

currentKeyText: Reduce metformin to 500 mg twice daily.
newKeyText: Continue metformin at the current dose.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Continue metformin at the current dose; eGFR 45 does not require a reduction.
• KDIGO 2022 and ADA SOC 2026 allow standard metformin dosing at eGFR 45 or higher with eGFR monitoring every 3-6 months; halve the dose (max 1,000 mg/day) only at eGFR 30-44 and stop below 30.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Reduce metformin to 500 mg twice daily**: Dose reduction applies at eGFR 30-44.
• **Switch to glipizide 5 mg daily**: A sulfonylurea adds hypoglycemia risk, especially in older adults with CKD.
• **Discontinue metformin and initiate insulin therapy**: Stopping metformin for insulin is unnecessary.
## Key takeaway
Metformin: full dose at eGFR 45+, max 1,000 mg/day at 30-44, stop below 30.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD; ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 11; metformin labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
Warfarin carries the greatest risk: amoxicillin can raise the INR and increase bleeding.
• Broad-spectrum penicillins can potentiate warfarin (altered gut vitamin K production), so the INR should be monitored when they are combined.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Probenecid**: Probenecid raises amoxicillin levels, an intentional, low-risk effect.
• **Metformin**: No meaningful metformin interaction.
• **Ibuprofen**: No clinically important ibuprofen interaction.
## Key takeaway
Check the INR when a warfarin patient starts an antibiotic.
(Guideline: Amoxicillin and warfarin labeling; CHEST antithrombotic guidance)

## Why this answer is correct
Switch lisinopril to losartan, which treats hypertension and HF without the ACE-inhibitor cough.
• ACE-inhibitor cough is bradykinin-mediated; an ARB keeps RAAS blockade for HF (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA). An ARNI is another option.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Amlodipine 5 mg daily**: Amlodipine has no HF outcome benefit and loses RAAS blockade.
• **Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily**: A thiazide does not replace RAAS inhibition in HF.
• **Diltiazem 120 mg daily**: Non-dihydropyridine CCBs such as diltiazem are harmful in HFrEF (Class 3: Harm).
## Key takeaway
ACE-inhibitor cough in HF: switch to an ARB (or ARNI).
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline)

currentKeyText: Current medications of metformin and glimepiride
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
The blood glucose of 220 mg/dL is the finding that needs follow-up.
• A glucose of 220 mg/dL on metformin plus glimepiride shows inadequate control and prompts A1c assessment and treatment intensification (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **eGFR of 60 mL/min**: EGFR 60 allows current therapy.
• **Current medications of metformin and glimepiride**: The regimen itself is not a finding.
• **Patient's concern about her regimen**: Her concern is addressed by acting on the hyperglycemia.
## Key takeaway
Act on the objective hyperglycemia.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

currentKeyText: Switch from metformin to a GLP-1 receptor agonist.
newKeyText: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor to his current medications.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Adding an SGLT2 inhibitor to metformin and glipizide is the best next step.
• ADA SOC 2026 recommends adding an agent with proven efficacy and low hypoglycemia risk (SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA) while continuing metformin; insulin is generally reserved for A1c above 10% or symptomatic hyperglycemia.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add insulin therapy to his regimen**: Insulin is not first choice at A1c 8.5% without catabolic symptoms.
• **Increase the dose of glipizide**: Raising glipizide increases hypoglycemia and weight gain.
• **Switch from metformin to a GLP-1 receptor agonist**: Metformin should be continued, not replaced.
## Key takeaway
Intensify by adding an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA to metformin.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 9)

currentKeyText: Take sumatriptan with food to improve absorption
newKeyText: Limit sumatriptan use to no more than 2 days per week
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Limit sumatriptan to no more than 2 days per week to prevent medication-overuse headache.
• Triptan use on 10 or more days per month causes medication-overuse headache (ICHD-3); frequent attacks warrant preventive therapy (AHS 2021).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase fluid intake to prevent dehydration**: Hydration is general advice, not the key safety point.
• **Take sumatriptan with food to improve absorption**: Food does not improve sumatriptan absorption.
• **Avoid triggers such as stress and certain foods**: Trigger avoidance helps but is less important than preventing overuse.
## Key takeaway
Triptans: fewer than 10 days per month (about 2 days per week).
(Guideline: American Headache Society 2021 consensus; ICHD-3 medication-overuse headache)

currentKeyText: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal.
newKeyText: Creatine kinase (CK) level greater than 5 times the upper limit of normal.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
A CK over 5 times the upper limit of normal with muscle pain warrants a change.
• With muscle symptoms, a markedly raised CK indicates statin myopathy; hold the statin and reassess (2018 ACC/AHA). His LFTs are normal.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal**: His LFTs are normal, so this value is not present.
• **Total cholesterol level greater than 240 mg/dL**: Total cholesterol is not a treatment target.
• **Blood pressure greater than 140/90 mmHg**: Blood pressure is not a laboratory value.
## Key takeaway
Statin muscle symptoms plus high CK: stop and reassess.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline; atorvastatin labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
The LDL of 160 mg/dL on atorvastatin 40 mg needs follow-up.
• An LDL of 160 mg/dL shows an inadequate response; assess adherence and intensify therapy (high-intensity statin, then add ezetimibe) (2018 ACC/AHA).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Elevated liver enzymes**: Her LFTs are normal.
• **History of muscle pain**: No muscle pain is reported.
• **Current use of grapefruit juice**: Grapefruit use is not described.
## Key takeaway
Follow up an LDL that remains high on statin therapy.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

currentKeyText: Ensure the child is well-hydrated while taking ibuprofen.
newKeyText: The maximum daily dose should not exceed 40 mg/kg.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Do not exceed 40 mg/kg/day of ibuprofen.
• Pediatric ibuprofen is 5-10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours, maximum 40 mg/kg/day (about 730 mg/day for this 18 kg child).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Ibuprofen can be given every 4 hours as needed**: Ibuprofen is dosed every 6-8 hours, not every 4 hours.
• **Ensure the child is well-hydrated while taking ibuprofen**: Hydration is reasonable but not the key dosing point.
• **Monitor for signs of gastrointestinal bleeding**: GI bleeding is rare with short-term pediatric use.
## Key takeaway
Pediatric ibuprofen: 10 mg/kg q6-8h, max 40 mg/kg/day.
(Guideline: Pediatric ibuprofen labeling; AAP fever guidance)

currentKeyText: Consult with the prescriber about adjusting the lisinopril dose.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Continue lisinopril and metformin without changes.
• At eGFR 45, KDIGO 2022 supports continuing an ACE inhibitor (kidney protection) and standard-dose metformin with eGFR monitoring every 3-6 months.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Consult with the prescriber about adjusting the lisinopril dose**: Lisinopril does not need dose adjustment for kidney function at eGFR 45.
• **Educate the patient on signs of worsening kidney function**: Education is useful but not the first action.
• **Switch metformin to an alternative diabetes medication**: Metformin is appropriate at eGFR 45.
## Key takeaway
Metformin and ACE inhibitors continue at eGFR 45.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD; ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 11)

currentKeyText: Liver function tests within normal limits
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
The A1c of 8.5% is the lab value that warrants a therapeutic change.
• An A1c above goal calls for intensification; her GI upset can be managed with extended-release metformin or taking it with food (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL**: SCr 0.9 is normal.
• **Liver function tests within normal limits**: Normal LFTs need no change.
• **Serum potassium 4.5 mEq/L**: K 4.5 is normal.
## Key takeaway
A1c above goal is the actionable lab.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6 and 9)

## Why this answer is correct
The potassium of 3.0 mEq/L warrants a change.
• Loop-diuretic hypokalemia raises arrhythmia risk in HF; replace potassium and consider an MRA while adjusting diuresis (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg**: 130/80 mm Hg is at goal.
• **Heart rate of 80 bpm**: Heart rate is not a laboratory value and 80 bpm is acceptable.
• **Weight gain of 2 kg**: Weight is not a laboratory value.
## Key takeaway
Correct hypokalemia in HF patients on loop diuretics.
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline)

newKeyText: Begin combination therapy with lisinopril and amlodipine.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Start two first-line agents, lisinopril plus amlodipine.
• Stage 2 hypertension (BP 140/90 or higher) warrants lifestyle changes plus two first-line drugs of different classes, preferably as a single-pill combination (2025 AHA/ACC).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Start lisinopril 10 mg daily / Start amlodipine 5 mg daily**: Monotherapy is unlikely to reach goal at 150/95.
• **Initiate lifestyle modifications only**: Lifestyle alone is for elevated BP or low-risk stage 1.
## Key takeaway
Stage 2 hypertension: start two first-line agents.
(Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline (and 2017 ACC/AHA))

## Why this answer is correct
Warfarin poses the greatest bleeding risk when added to aspirin plus clopidogrel.
• Adding an anticoagulant to dual antiplatelet therapy (triple therapy) markedly increases major bleeding; it is used only with a clear indication and for the shortest time.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Ibuprofen**: NSAIDs also raise bleeding risk, but less than an anticoagulant.
• **Simvastatin**: Simvastatin has no significant clopidogrel interaction.
• **Metoprolol**: Metoprolol does not interact.
## Key takeaway
Triple antithrombotic therapy carries the highest bleeding risk.
(Guideline: 2023 ACC/AHA chronic coronary disease guideline; clopidogrel labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
The elevated HbA1c of 9.0% needs follow-up.
• An A1c of 9.0% on metformin is well above goal and warrants adding another agent (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Weight gain / Hypoglycemia / Increased thirst**: Weight gain, hypoglycemia and thirst are not reported in this case.
## Key takeaway
The A1c above goal is the finding to act on.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

currentKeyText: Refer to a cardiologist for further evaluation
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Increase furosemide to 80 mg daily to treat her fluid overload.
• Weight gain and edema indicate congestion; the loop diuretic dose should be increased to relieve it (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add spironolactone to her regimen**: Spironolactone is GDMT for HFrEF but is not a decongestion strategy and raises hyperkalemia risk in CKD.
• **Switch to torsemide 20 mg daily**: Switching to torsemide may help later but increasing the current dose is first.
• **Refer to a cardiologist for further evaluation**: Referral delays simple treatment.
## Key takeaway
Congestion in HF: increase the loop diuretic.
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
The elevated A1c of 7.8% is the finding to follow up.
• An A1c of 7.8% on metformin is above the usual <7% goal and supports adding therapy (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Signs of hypoglycemia / Increased thirst and urination / Weight gain**: Hypoglycemia, polyuria/polydipsia and weight gain are not described in the case.
## Key takeaway
Act on the A1c above goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

## Why this answer is correct
Start spironolactone at 25 mg daily.
• For HFrEF with eGFR above 50 and K 5.0 or lower, the guideline starting dose is 25 mg daily (12.5 mg daily or every other day if eGFR 31-49); check K and SCr within 1 week.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **12.5 mg daily**: 12.5 mg is for eGFR 31-49.
• **50 mg daily / 100 mg daily**: 50-100 mg raises hyperkalemia risk, especially with lisinopril.
## Key takeaway
Spironolactone in HF: 25 mg daily if eGFR above 50 and K 5.0 or lower.
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline)

currentKeyText: Desire to start a new medication
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
The A1c of 7.8% is the finding that needs follow-up.
• An A1c above the <7% goal on metformin monotherapy supports adding another agent (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Current metformin use**: Metformin should continue.
• **Desire to start a new medication**: Her wish is addressed by acting on the A1c.
• **No renal impairment**: Normal renal function is reassuring.
## Key takeaway
Act on the A1c above goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

## Why this answer is correct
Fluticasone nasal spray is the most effective choice for sneezing, congestion and itchy eyes.
• Intranasal corticosteroids are first-line for allergic rhinitis and relieve nasal congestion and ocular symptoms better than oral antihistamines (2020 practice parameter); they do not raise BP.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Diphenhydramine**: Diphenhydramine is sedating and anticholinergic.
• **Loratadine**: Loratadine does little for congestion.
• **Pseudoephedrine**: Pseudoephedrine can raise blood pressure in a patient with hypertension.
## Key takeaway
Allergic rhinitis with congestion: intranasal corticosteroid first.
(Guideline: AAAAI/ACAAI 2020 rhinitis practice parameter)

currentKeyText: Ondansetron is safe to use during pregnancy
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Take ondansetron about 30 minutes before chemotherapy.
• 5-HT3 antagonists work best as prophylaxis given before chemotherapy (ASCO 2020); oral ondansetron is given 30 minutes before treatment.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Take ondansetron only when nausea occurs**: Waiting for nausea reduces effectiveness.
• **Ondansetron can cause sedation**: Headache and constipation are typical, not sedation.
• **Ondansetron is safe to use during pregnancy**: Pregnancy safety is not relevant for this patient.
## Key takeaway
Antiemetics for chemotherapy are given before the dose.
(Guideline: ASCO 2020 antiemetic guideline; ondansetron labeling)

currentKeyText: Switch amlodipine to losartan 50 mg daily.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Add lisinopril 10 mg daily.
• BP 150/95 on amlodipine is above the <130/80 goal; adding an ACE inhibitor is preferred in diabetes (ADA SOC 2026), giving a two-drug regimen.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase metformin to 2000 mg daily**: He already takes metformin 2,000 mg/day (1,000 mg twice daily).
• **Add glipizide 5 mg daily**: Glipizide does not address the uncontrolled BP.
• **Switch amlodipine to losartan 50 mg daily**: Swapping one drug for another keeps him on monotherapy.
## Key takeaway
Uncontrolled BP in diabetes: add an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
(Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline; ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 10)

## Why this answer is correct
Check a lipid panel 4-12 weeks after the dose change.
• The guideline assesses adherence and LDL response with a fasting or nonfasting lipid panel 4-12 weeks after starting or changing a statin, then every 3-12 months.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Liver function tests in 6 weeks**: Routine liver tests are not recommended after a statin change unless symptoms occur.
• **Creatinine clearance every month**: Monthly creatinine clearance is unnecessary.
• **Blood pressure weekly**: Weekly BP is unrelated to the statin.
## Key takeaway
After a statin change, recheck lipids in 4-12 weeks; no routine LFTs.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

currentKeyText: Recommend a vitamin D3 supplement of 1000 IU daily.
newKeyText: Refer her to her primary care provider for further evaluation.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Refer her to her primary care provider for evaluation and repletion.
• A 25(OH)D of 15 ng/mL is deficient, and with muscle weakness and osteoporosis she needs clinician-directed repletion (typically higher-dose therapy) and evaluation.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Recommend a vitamin D3 supplement of 1000 IU daily**: 1,000 IU daily is maintenance, not repletion.
• **Advise her to increase sun exposure for vitamin D synthesis**: Sun exposure is unreliable and not recommended as treatment.
• **Suggest a higher dose of alendronate for osteoporosis**: Alendronate 70 mg weekly is the standard dose.
## Key takeaway
Symptomatic vitamin D deficiency needs clinician-directed repletion.
(Guideline: Endocrine Society 2024 vitamin D guideline; BHOF 2022)

currentKeyText: Ibuprofen should be taken with food to minimize gastrointestinal upset.
newKeyText: The maximum daily dose should not exceed 40 mg/kg.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Do not exceed 40 mg/kg/day of ibuprofen.
• Pediatric ibuprofen is 5-10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours with a maximum of 40 mg/kg/day.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Ibuprofen can be given every 4 hours as needed**: Ibuprofen is given every 6-8 hours, not every 4 hours.
• **Ibuprofen should be taken with food to minimize gastrointestinal upset**: Taking it with food is reasonable but not the key dosing safeguard.
• **It is safe to give ibuprofen and amoxicillin together**: True but not about dosing.
## Key takeaway
Pediatric ibuprofen: max 40 mg/kg/day.
(Guideline: Pediatric ibuprofen labeling; AAP fever guidance)

currentKeyText: You should take alendronate only when you have symptoms of osteoporosis.
newKeyText: Remain upright for at least 30 minutes after taking alendronate.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Remain upright for at least 30 minutes after taking alendronate.
• Take alendronate first thing in the morning with 6-8 oz of plain water on an empty stomach, and stay upright for 30 minutes to reduce esophageal irritation.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Take alendronate with food to improve absorption**: Food markedly reduces absorption.
• **You can take alendronate at any time of day**: It must be taken in the morning before food.
• **You should take alendronate only when you have symptoms of osteoporosis**: It is daily/weekly preventive therapy, not symptom-based.
## Key takeaway
Alendronate: empty stomach, plain water, upright 30 minutes.
(Guideline: Alendronate labeling; BHOF 2022)

newKeyText: Continue apixaban at the same dose.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily.
• Dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily needs 2 of 3 criteria (age 80+, weight 60 kg or less, SCr 1.5+); he meets only SCr. Falls alone are not a reason to stop anticoagulation (2023 AF guideline).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase apixaban to 10 mg daily**: 10 mg daily is not an AF regimen.
• **Switch to warfarin**: Warfarin offers no advantage and more bleeding.
• **Discontinue anticoagulation therapy**: Stopping leaves him unprotected against stroke.
## Key takeaway
Apixaban: 2 of 3 (80, 60, 1.5) before reducing.
(Guideline: Apixaban labeling; 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline)

currentKeyText: Switch to a combination inhaler with a LABA and inhaled corticosteroid
newKeyText: Add a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) to her regimen
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Add a LABA to tiotropium (LAMA/LABA).
• GOLD 2025 recommends escalating to LAMA/LABA for persistent dyspnea on a single long-acting bronchodilator.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase the dose of tiotropium**: Tiotropium has a fixed dose.
• **Switch to a combination inhaler with a LABA and inhaled corticosteroid**: ICS/LABA is not recommended without exacerbations or eosinophilia, and ICS raises pneumonia risk.
• **Add a leukotriene receptor antagonist**: Leukotriene antagonists have no role in COPD.
## Key takeaway
Persistent dyspnea on a LAMA: add a LABA.
(Guideline: GOLD 2025)

## Why this answer is correct
Canagliflozin 100 mg daily is the best choice given his CKD.
• KDIGO 2022 recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor in T2D with eGFR 20 or higher for kidney and CV protection; canagliflozin is limited to 100 mg at eGFR below 60.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Glipizide 5 mg daily**: Glipizide raises hypoglycemia risk in older adults with CKD.
• **Sitagliptin 100 mg daily**: Sitagliptin must be reduced to 50 mg at eGFR 30-44.
• **Insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime**: Insulin is not needed.
## Key takeaway
T2D with CKD: SGLT2 inhibitor.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD; canagliflozin labeling)

currentKeyText: Discontinue atorvastatin and recommend a non-statin alternative.
newKeyText: Switch atorvastatin to rosuvastatin at a lower dose.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Switch to a lower dose of a different statin (rosuvastatin).
• For statin-associated muscle symptoms without severe features, the guideline advises reassessing and rechallenging with a lower dose or different statin; mild transaminase elevations under 3 times ULN do not require stopping.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Continue atorvastatin and monitor liver function tests in 6 months**: Continuing unchanged ignores his symptoms.
• **Counsel the patient to take atorvastatin at bedtime**: Atorvastatin timing does not affect muscle symptoms.
• **Discontinue atorvastatin and recommend a non-statin alternative**: Non-statins are considered only after statin intolerance is confirmed.
## Key takeaway
Statin muscle symptoms: reassess, then rechallenge at a lower dose or different statin.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
Combining tiotropium with an antihistamine adds anticholinergic effects.
• Tiotropium labeling warns against combining it with other anticholinergic drugs because of additive effects (urinary retention, dry mouth, constipation); first-generation antihistamines are anticholinergic.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Tiotropium with a beta-blocker**: Beta-blockers interact with beta-agonists, not tiotropium.
• **Tiotropium with an oral corticosteroid**: Oral corticosteroids have no significant interaction.
• **Tiotropium with a long-acting beta-agonist**: LAMA/LABA is an intended combination.
## Key takeaway
Avoid stacking anticholinergics with tiotropium.
(Guideline: Tiotropium labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
The 5-pound weight gain in a week needs follow-up.
• Rapid weight gain (more than 2-3 lb in a day or 5 lb in a week) signals fluid retention in HF and warrants diuretic adjustment.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Fatigue**: Fatigue is nonspecific.
• **Blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg**: 135/85 mm Hg needs no urgent change.
• **Current medications**: The medication list is not a finding.
## Key takeaway
Weight gain of 5 lb in a week signals HF decompensation.
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
The serum creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL warrants a change.
• In a 67-year-old woman SCr 1.8 gives an eGFR of about 30 (CKD-EPI 2021); metformin must be reduced to a maximum of 1,000 mg/day at eGFR 30-44 (KDIGO 2022).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Potassium 5.5 mEq/L / Blood glucose 180 mg/dL**: K 5.5 and glucose 180 are not reported in the case.
• **Blood pressure 150/90 mmHg**: Blood pressure is not a laboratory value.
## Key takeaway
Recheck metformin dose when eGFR falls below 45.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD; metformin labeling)

currentKeyText: Switch to a high-dose inhaled corticosteroid.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Increase the budesonide/formoterol dose (step up ICS-formoterol therapy).
• Albuterol use more than twice weekly with night waking means uncontrolled asthma; GINA 2024/25 steps up ICS-formoterol to medium-dose maintenance-and-reliever therapy.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add montelukast 10 mg daily**: Montelukast is a less effective add-on with a boxed neuropsychiatric warning.
• **Switch to a high-dose inhaled corticosteroid**: Switching to ICS alone removes the LABA.
• **Add a long-acting beta-agonist**: She already receives a LABA (formoterol), so adding another duplicates therapy.
## Key takeaway
Uncontrolled on ICS-formoterol: step up the ICS-formoterol dose.
(Guideline: GINA 2024/2025)

currentKeyText: Inform her that green tea extract may reduce the effectiveness of her contraceptive.
newKeyText: Suggest she consult her physician before starting any new supplement.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Advise her to check with her physician before starting the supplement.
• Green tea extract has no proven effect on contraceptive efficacy, but concentrated extracts have been linked to liver injury (USP), and weight-loss supplements are unregulated; clinician review is prudent.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Advise her to stop taking the oral contraceptives**: There is no reason to stop her contraceptive.
• **Inform her that green tea extract may reduce the effectiveness of her contraceptive**: Green tea extract is not known to reduce contraceptive effectiveness.
• **Reassure her that green tea extract is safe with oral contraceptives**: It is not risk-free because of hepatotoxicity reports.
## Key takeaway
Green tea extract: no OC interaction, but liver-injury risk warrants review.
(Guideline: NIH ODS green tea monograph; USP hepatotoxicity advisory)

## Why this answer is correct
The potassium of 5.8 mEq/L warrants a change.
• K 5.8 on lisinopril is significant hyperkalemia; the RAAS inhibitor dose and potassium sources must be addressed (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Creatinine level of 1.5 mg/dL**: SCr 1.5 is a modest value without a baseline.
• **Sodium level of 130 mEq/L**: Na 130 is mild hyponatremia common in HF.
• **B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) of 300 pg/mL**: A BNP of 300 is consistent with the known congestion.
## Key takeaway
Hyperkalemia above 5.5 on a RAAS inhibitor requires action.
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline; KDIGO 2024 hyperkalemia)

currentKeyText: Take alendronate with a full glass of water
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Stop alendronate and contact the prescriber.
• Labeling says to discontinue alendronate and seek medical attention if dysphagia, odynophagia, retrosternal pain or new or worsening heartburn develop, because of esophageal injury risk.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Take alendronate with a full glass of water**: Correct technique prevents injury but does not treat active symptoms.
• **Switch to a different bisphosphonate**: Other oral bisphosphonates carry the same esophageal risk.
• **Take alendronate at bedtime**: Bedtime dosing increases reflux and injury.
## Key takeaway
Esophageal symptoms on alendronate: stop and refer.
(Guideline: Alendronate labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
The risk of QT prolongation is the finding to address.
• Azithromycin carries an FDA warning for QT prolongation and fatal arrhythmia; it has minimal CYP3A4 inhibition, so it does not meaningfully raise atorvastatin levels.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Potential for increased atorvastatin levels**: Azithromycin, unlike clarithromycin, does not significantly raise atorvastatin levels.
• **Increased risk of gastrointestinal side effects**: GI effects are common but not serious.
• **Risk of acute kidney injury**: Azithromycin is not nephrotoxic.
## Key takeaway
Azithromycin: QT risk, not CYP3A4 inhibition.
(Guideline: Azithromycin labeling (FDA 2013 QT warning))

## Why this answer is correct
The elevated A1c of 9.0% needs follow-up.
• An A1c of 9.0% on metformin is well above goal and warrants adding therapy (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increased thirst / Weight loss / Fatigue**: Thirst, weight loss and fatigue are not described in the case.
## Key takeaway
Act on the A1c above goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

## Why this answer is correct
The elevated A1c of 7.8% needs follow-up.
• An A1c above goal on metformin supports adding an agent, ideally one that also helps weight (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Weight gain**: Weight gain is not reported.
• **Increased thirst / Frequent urination**: Thirst and urination are not described.
## Key takeaway
Act on the A1c above goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

## Why this answer is correct
The blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg needs follow-up.
• BP 140/90 is above the <130/80 goal for a patient with HF and diabetes; her lisinopril should continue and therapy be intensified.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **eGFR of 55 mL/min**: EGFR 55 does not require changes.
• **Current medications including atorvastatin**: Atorvastatin is appropriate.
• **History of heart failure**: Her HF history is background, not a new finding.
## Key takeaway
BP above 130/80 in HF and diabetes needs intensification.
(Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA)

## Why this answer is correct
Her persistent muscle pain and weakness need follow-up.
• Statin-associated muscle symptoms should prompt evaluation (CK, other causes) and a statin hold or change (2018 ACC/AHA).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increased liver enzymes / Elevated creatine kinase (CK) levels**: No liver enzyme or CK results are given.
• **Newly developed hypertension**: Hypertension is not new.
## Key takeaway
Evaluate muscle symptoms in a statin user.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

currentKeyText: Blood glucose levels consistently above 180 mg/dL.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
The A1c above 7% (7.5%) is the value that warrants a change.
• His A1c of 7.5% is above the usual <7% goal, which supports treatment intensification (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Blood glucose levels consistently above 180 mg/dL**: Glucose readings above 180 are not reported.
• **Serum creatinine above 1.5 mg/dL**: His renal function is normal.
• **Lipid panel showing LDL greater than 100 mg/dL**: No LDL result is given.
## Key takeaway
Use the reported A1c against goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

currentKeyText: Consider a supplement containing green tea extract.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Orlistat is the only FDA-approved OTC weight-loss product among the options.
• Orlistat 60 mg (Alli) is FDA-approved OTC with proven modest weight loss when combined with diet.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Consider a supplement containing green tea extract**: Green tea extract lacks proven efficacy and is linked to liver injury.
• **Try a supplement with ephedra**: Ephedra was banned by the FDA in 2004.
• **Choose a supplement with caffeine**: Caffeine supplements lack proven efficacy and raise BP and heart rate.
## Key takeaway
The evidence-based OTC weight-loss choice is orlistat.
(Guideline: FDA OTC approval of orlistat (Alli))

## Why this answer is correct
The 5-pound weight gain in a week needs follow-up.
• Rapid weight gain signals fluid retention in HF and warrants diuretic adjustment.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Blood pressure of 130/80 mm Hg**: 130/80 mm Hg is acceptable.
• **Heart rate of 70 bpm**: 70 bpm is at target.
• **Fatigue reported by the patient**: Fatigue is nonspecific.
## Key takeaway
Weight gain of 5 lb in a week signals HF decompensation.
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline)

currentKeyText: Contact the prescriber to clarify the beyond-use date.
newKeyText: Dispense the cream with a standard beyond-use date of 30 days.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
The pharmacist assigns the BUD and dispenses with it.
• Under USP <795> the compounding pharmacist assigns the BUD from stability data or USP default limits; the prescriber does not supply it. (Current USP <795> default for a preserved aqueous topical is 35 days.)
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Contact the prescriber to clarify the beyond-use date**: BUDs are not the prescriber's responsibility.
• **Inform the patient that the cream is safe to use indefinitely**: Compounded preparations are never indefinite.
• **Provide the patient with a warning about potential contamination**: A warning does not replace a BUD.
## Key takeaway
The compounder assigns the BUD per USP <795>.
(Guideline: USP <795> Nonsterile Compounding)

## Why this answer is correct
The eGFR of 45 mL/min needs follow-up monitoring.
• At eGFR 45 metformin may continue at full dose, but eGFR should be rechecked every 3-6 months; halve the dose if it falls below 45 and stop below 30 (KDIGO 2022).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increased blood glucose levels / Weight gain / Nausea and vomiting**: Hyperglycemia, weight gain and nausea are not reported.
## Key takeaway
Metformin at eGFR 45: continue and monitor eGFR every 3-6 months.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD; metformin labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
Switch lisinopril to losartan.
• Her persistent cough is most likely from the ACE inhibitor; an ARB keeps the RAAS blockade recommended in diabetes without the bradykinin-mediated cough.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Amlodipine 5 mg daily / Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily**: They do not replace RAAS blockade in diabetes.
• **Diltiazem 120 mg daily**: Diltiazem is not preferred for hypertension in diabetes.
## Key takeaway
ACE-inhibitor cough: switch to an ARB.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 10; 2025 AHA/ACC)

## Why this answer is correct
Fish oil provides EPA/DHA and has no interaction with oral contraceptives.
• Marine omega-3s (EPA/DHA) are the form with cardiovascular evidence; they do not affect contraceptive efficacy.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Flaxseed oil supplements**: Flaxseed provides ALA, which converts poorly to EPA/DHA.
• **Coenzyme Q10**: CoQ10 is not an omega-3.
• **Ginkgo biloba**: Ginkgo is not an omega-3 and raises bleeding risk.
## Key takeaway
For omega-3s, choose fish oil (EPA/DHA).
(Guideline: AHA omega-3 scientific statement)

## Why this answer is correct
Continue the current medications; bupropion does not add serotonergic activity.
• Bupropion is a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor, so combining it with sertraline does not meaningfully raise serotonin syndrome risk; it is a common augmentation strategy (watch seizure risk and CYP2D6 inhibition).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase the dose of sertraline**: A higher sertraline dose increases serotonergic load.
• **Switch to fluoxetine**: Switching SSRIs does not reduce risk.
• **Add trazodone**: Trazodone is serotonergic and adds risk.
## Key takeaway
Bupropion is not serotonergic.
(Guideline: Bupropion and sertraline labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
Switch lisinopril to losartan.
• Persistent cough on lisinopril is most likely ACE-inhibitor cough; an ARB keeps the RAAS blockade recommended in diabetes.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Amlodipine 5 mg daily / Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily**: They do not replace RAAS blockade in diabetes.
• **Metoprolol 50 mg daily**: Beta-blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension.
## Key takeaway
ACE-inhibitor cough: switch to an ARB.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 10; 2025 AHA/ACC)

## Why this answer is correct
Canagliflozin (an SGLT2 inhibitor) is the best alternative in a patient with heart failure.
• SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF hospitalization and are recommended in T2D with HF (ADA SOC 2026; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA); eGFR 55 permits use.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Sitagliptin**: Sitagliptin is HF-neutral without benefit (avoid saxagliptin/alogliptin).
• **Insulin aspart**: Prandial insulin is not an initial choice.
• **Pioglitazone**: Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and is contraindicated in symptomatic HF.
## Key takeaway
Diabetes with HF: choose an SGLT2 inhibitor.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 9/10; 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA)

## Why this answer is correct
The A1c of 7.8% needs follow-up.
• An A1c above the usual <7% goal supports intensifying therapy (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL**: SCr 1.2 is not concerning.
• **Current medications**: The regimen is appropriate.
• **Blood pressure readings**: No BP readings are given.
## Key takeaway
Act on the A1c above goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

## Why this answer is correct
Ezetimibe 10 mg daily is the appropriate add-on.
• Ezetimibe is the recommended first non-statin add-on when LDL remains high on statin therapy, and it is well tolerated (2018 ACC/AHA).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Simvastatin 20 mg daily**: Simvastatin duplicates statin therapy.
• **Fenofibrate 145 mg daily**: Fenofibrate targets triglycerides.
• **Niacin 500 mg daily**: Niacin adds side effects without outcome benefit.
## Key takeaway
First non-statin add-on for LDL: ezetimibe.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

currentKeyText: Take another dose of sumatriptan after 1 hour if needed
newKeyText: Do not take more than 200 mg of sumatriptan in 24 hours
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Do not take more than 200 mg of oral sumatriptan in 24 hours.
• If the migraine returns or does not fully resolve, a second dose may be taken at least 2 hours after the first, up to 200 mg per 24 hours.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Take another dose of sumatriptan after 1 hour if needed**: The repeat interval is 2 hours, not 1.
• **Take sumatriptan with food to enhance absorption**: Food does not enhance absorption.
• **Avoid using sumatriptan more than twice a week**: Frequency limits matter for overuse, but her question is about re-dosing.
## Key takeaway
Oral sumatriptan: repeat after 2 hours, max 200 mg/day.
(Guideline: Sumatriptan labeling)

currentKeyText: She has a history of liver disease.
newKeyText: Her LDL is above the target range.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Her LDL above target needs follow-up.
• An LDL of 160 mg/dL on atorvastatin shows inadequate response; assess adherence and intensify therapy (2018 ACC/AHA).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **She is taking atorvastatin with lisinopril**: Atorvastatin and lisinopril do not interact.
• **She has a history of liver disease**: No liver disease is described.
• **Her blood pressure is well controlled**: Controlled BP is not a problem.
## Key takeaway
Follow up an LDL above goal on statin therapy.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
Start oral corticosteroids for this moderate-to-severe exacerbation.
• PEF 60% of best with wheeze on ICS/LABA is an exacerbation; GINA recommends repeated SABA plus a short course of oral corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone 40-50 mg for 5-7 days).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase the dose of fluticasone/salmeterol**: Increasing the controller does not treat an acute exacerbation adequately.
• **Add a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA)**: He already takes a LABA.
• **Prescribe a leukotriene receptor antagonist**: Montelukast has no role in acute exacerbations.
## Key takeaway
Acute asthma exacerbation: SABA plus systemic corticosteroids.
(Guideline: GINA 2024/2025)

## Why this answer is correct
Recommend celecoxib, a non-opioid analgesic for osteoarthritis.
• ACR 2019 strongly recommends oral NSAIDs for OA and advises against escalating opioids; CDC 2022 favors maximizing non-opioid therapy. Monitor BP and renal function with lisinopril.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours**: Escalating to oxycodone raises opioid risks without better OA outcomes.
• **Tramadol 50 mg every 6 hours**: Tramadol is still an opioid with serotonergic and seizure risks.
• **Methadone 5 mg every 8 hours**: Methadone is not appropriate for this indication and carries QT and accumulation risks.
## Key takeaway
Chronic OA pain: optimize non-opioids (NSAID) before opioids.
(Guideline: ACR 2019 osteoarthritis guideline; CDC 2022 opioid guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
The 2 kg weight gain in a week needs follow-up.
• Rapid weight gain signals fluid retention in HF and warrants diuretic adjustment.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Fatigue**: Fatigue is nonspecific.
• **Stable eGFR of 45 mL/min**: A stable eGFR needs no action.
• **Current medications**: The medication list is not a finding.
## Key takeaway
Weight gain of 2 kg in a week signals HF decompensation.
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
The severity of her muscle pain needs follow-up.
• Statin-associated muscle symptoms should be assessed for severity, with CK checked if severe, and the statin held or changed (2018 ACC/AHA).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Elevated liver enzymes / Increased creatinine levels / Change in lipid panel results**: No liver, creatinine or lipid changes are reported.
## Key takeaway
Assess muscle symptoms in statin users.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
Switch lisinopril to losartan.
• A dry cough on lisinopril is typical ACE-inhibitor cough; an ARB keeps RAAS blockade recommended in diabetes.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Amlodipine 5 mg daily / Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily**: They do not replace RAAS blockade.
• **Diltiazem 120 mg daily**: Diltiazem is not preferred for hypertension.
## Key takeaway
ACE-inhibitor cough: switch to an ARB.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 10)

## Why this answer is correct
Add an SGLT2 inhibitor such as empagliflozin.
• SGLT2 inhibitors lower A1c and cause modest weight loss without hypoglycemia (ADA SOC 2026); a GLP-1 RA would also fit but is not offered.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Insulin glargine**: Insulin causes weight gain.
• **Thiazolidinedione (e.g., pioglitazone)**: Pioglitazone causes weight gain and edema.
• **DPP-4 inhibitor (e.g., sitagliptin)**: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral with less A1c lowering.
## Key takeaway
To avoid weight gain, add an SGLT2 inhibitor (or GLP-1 RA).
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 9)

## Why this answer is correct
Check creatine kinase because he reports muscle aches.
• In a statin user with muscle symptoms, CK helps distinguish myopathy (2018 ACC/AHA); routine liver monitoring is not recommended.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Liver function tests (LFTs)**: Routine LFTs are not needed without liver symptoms.
• **Lipid panel**: The lipid panel guides efficacy, but the safety signal is the muscle aches.
• **Blood pressure**: BP is unrelated to the statin.
## Key takeaway
Statin muscle symptoms: check CK.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
The eGFR of 45 mL/min must be considered in choosing and monitoring therapy.
• eGFR 45 is CKD stage 3a; it favors adding an SGLT2 inhibitor, requires dose adjustment of some agents (e.g., DPP-4 inhibitors) and eGFR monitoring every 3-6 months (KDIGO 2022).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Current medications**: The current regimen is appropriate.
• **Blood glucose levels / Blood pressure readings**: No glucose or BP readings are given.
## Key takeaway
eGFR drives drug selection and dosing in diabetes.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD)

## Why this answer is correct
Switch to acetaminophen.
• NSAIDs cause sodium and fluid retention (edema) and blunt ACE-inhibitor effects; acetaminophen avoids these problems.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Naproxen / Celecoxib**: Naproxen and celecoxib also cause edema and raise BP.
• **Aspirin**: Analgesic-dose aspirin has the same NSAID effects plus GI bleeding.
## Key takeaway
NSAID-induced edema: switch to acetaminophen.
(Guideline: ACR 2019 osteoarthritis guideline; 2025 AHA/ACC)

## Why this answer is correct
Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily.
• He meets only one criterion (age 72 does not count; no weight or SCr at threshold given), so the standard 5 mg twice-daily AF dose is correct; CrCl 45 alone is not a reduction criterion.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Warfarin with INR monitoring**: Warfarin offers no advantage.
• **Rivaroxaban 15 mg once daily**: Switching to rivaroxaban is unnecessary.
• **Dabigatran 110 mg twice daily**: Dabigatran 110 mg is not a US-approved AF dose.
## Key takeaway
Apixaban: reduce only with 2 of 3 criteria.
(Guideline: Apixaban labeling; 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline)

currentKeyText: Weight gain of 2 pounds in one week
newKeyText: Blood glucose levels consistently above 180 mg/dL
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Glucose readings consistently above 180 mg/dL need follow-up.
• Pregnancy targets are fasting <95 mg/dL and 1-h postprandial <140 or 2-h <120 mg/dL; readings above 180 mean GDM is uncontrolled and insulin (preferred in pregnancy) should be considered (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Weight gain of 2 pounds in one week**: 2 lb in a week is within expected pregnancy gain.
• **Nausea and vomiting**: Nausea is common in pregnancy and with metformin but is not the priority.
• **Increased thirst**: Thirst alone is nonspecific.
## Key takeaway
GDM above target: intensify, preferably with insulin.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 15)

## Why this answer is correct
The eGFR of 45 mL/min needs follow-up.
• eGFR 45 requires monitoring every 3-6 months and review of renally cleared drugs; metformin may continue at full dose but must be halved if eGFR falls below 45 (KDIGO 2022).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Current medications**: Her regimen is appropriate.
• **Blood pressure reading / Cholesterol levels**: No BP or lipid results are given.
## Key takeaway
eGFR 45 on metformin: continue and monitor closely.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD)

## Why this answer is correct
Lisinopril 20 mg daily is the best choice.
• For hypertension with CKD, an ACE inhibitor or ARB is preferred (especially with albuminuria) (KDIGO 2021); check K and SCr in 1-2 weeks.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Amlodipine 5 mg daily / Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily / Metoprolol 50 mg daily**: Amlodipine, HCTZ and metoprolol lack the kidney-protective effect of RAAS blockade in CKD.
## Key takeaway
Hypertension with CKD: ACE inhibitor or ARB first.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2021 BP in CKD; 2025 AHA/ACC)

currentKeyText: I want to avoid medications that may raise my blood pressure.
newKeyText: I plan to take the medication only when my symptoms are severe.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
The plan to use medication only when symptoms are severe needs correction.
• Intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines work best when used regularly during allergy season; waiting for severe symptoms gives poor control.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **I prefer a non-drowsy option for my allergies**: A non-drowsy preference is reasonable.
• **I have tried antihistamines before without any issues**: Prior tolerance is useful information.
• **I want to avoid medications that may raise my blood pressure**: Avoiding decongestants with hypertension is correct.
## Key takeaway
Allergy medications work best when taken regularly in season.
(Guideline: AAAAI/ACAAI 2020 rhinitis practice parameter)

## Why this answer is correct
The A1c of 9.2% needs follow-up.
• An A1c of 9.2% on metformin plus glipizide is far above goal and requires intensification (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Fatigue**: Fatigue is nonspecific.
• **Current medications**: The regimen itself is not a finding.
• **History of diabetes**: Her diabetes history is background.
## Key takeaway
Act on the A1c above goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

currentKeyText: Switch to a different inhaled corticosteroid
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Step up by increasing the fluticasone/salmeterol (ICS) dose.
• SABA use more than twice weekly with night waking means uncontrolled asthma; GINA steps up to a higher ICS-LABA dose (or ICS-formoterol MART) after checking technique and adherence.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add montelukast 10 mg daily**: Montelukast is a less effective add-on with a boxed neuropsychiatric warning.
• **Switch to a different inhaled corticosteroid**: Changing ICS without raising the dose does not step up therapy.
• **Add a long-acting beta-agonist**: She already takes a LABA (salmeterol).
## Key takeaway
Uncontrolled on ICS-LABA: check technique, then step up the dose.
(Guideline: GINA 2024/2025)

currentKeyText: Continue atorvastatin at the same dose.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Increase atorvastatin to 80 mg daily.
• She is adherent without side effects and LDL is 160 mg/dL on a moderate dose; the guideline maximizes statin intensity before adding a non-statin.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add ezetimibe to her regimen**: Ezetimibe is added after maximal tolerated statin.
• **Switch atorvastatin to rosuvastatin**: Switching to rosuvastatin at an unstated dose is not clearly an intensification.
• **Continue atorvastatin at the same dose**: Continuing leaves LDL uncontrolled.
## Key takeaway
Maximize the statin before adding a non-statin.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

currentKeyText: Discontinue lisinopril and start metoprolol 50 mg daily.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Switch lisinopril to amlodipine 5 mg daily.
• Her persistent cough is an ACE-inhibitor effect, so lisinopril should stop; among the options amlodipine is a first-line agent (an ARB would also be reasonable if offered).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase lisinopril to 20 mg daily**: A higher lisinopril dose worsens the cough.
• **Add hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily**: Adding HCTZ leaves the cough-causing drug.
• **Discontinue lisinopril and start metoprolol 50 mg daily**: Metoprolol is not first-line for hypertension.
## Key takeaway
ACE-inhibitor cough: stop the ACE inhibitor.
(Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
Migraine frequency is the most critical parameter to monitor.
• Migraine on 4-5 days per week signals medication-overuse risk and the need for preventive therapy (AHS 2021).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Liver function tests (LFTs)**: Sumatriptan does not require liver monitoring.
• **Blood pressure**: BP matters for triptans but is not the key issue here.
• **Serum electrolytes**: Electrolytes are not affected.
## Key takeaway
Frequent migraine: track frequency and start prevention.
(Guideline: AHS 2021 consensus statement)

currentKeyText: The inhaler can be stored in a hot car without affecting its effectiveness.
newKeyText: Inhale deeply and hold your breath for 10 seconds after using the inhaler.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Inhale slowly and deeply, then hold the breath for about 10 seconds after the puff.
• Correct pMDI technique (with a spacer for a young child) delivers drug to the lungs; a breath-hold of up to 10 seconds improves deposition.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Use the inhaler only when the child is experiencing an asthma attack**: Albuterol is used for symptoms and before exercise, not only during attacks.
• **The inhaler can be stored in a hot car without affecting its effectiveness**: Heat can damage the canister and dose.
• **The child should use the inhaler every day, even if she feels fine**: Daily use regardless of symptoms describes a controller, not albuterol.
## Key takeaway
Teach correct MDI technique with a spacer and breath-hold.
(Guideline: GINA 2024/2025; NAEPP 2020)

## Why this answer is correct
The potassium of 5.5 mEq/L warrants a change.
• K 5.5 on an ACE inhibitor with CKD needs action (dietary review, potassium binder or RAAS dose reduction) (KDIGO 2024).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Sodium level of 135 mEq/L**: Na 135 is normal.
• **Creatinine level of 1.8 mg/dL**: SCr 1.8 is consistent with her known CKD.
• **BUN level of 20 mg/dL**: BUN 20 is normal.
## Key takeaway
Address hyperkalemia on RAAS inhibitors.
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA; KDIGO 2024 CKD)

## Why this answer is correct
Switch lisinopril to losartan 50 mg daily.
• Her dry cough is an ACE-inhibitor effect; an ARB maintains RAAS blockade for CKD without the cough.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Amlodipine 10 mg daily**: Higher-dose amlodipine adds edema and worsens orthostasis.
• **Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily**: HCTZ 25 mg may worsen orthostatic dizziness.
• **Metoprolol 50 mg daily**: Metoprolol is not first-line.
## Key takeaway
ACE-inhibitor cough with CKD: switch to an ARB.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2021 BP in CKD; 2025 AHA/ACC)

## Why this answer is correct
The elevated A1c of 8.5% needs follow-up.
• An A1c of 8.5% on metformin requires intensification (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Normal renal function**: Normal renal function is reassuring.
• **Interest in cardiovascular benefits**: Her interest is addressed by choosing an agent.
• **Current medication adherence**: No adherence problem is described.
## Key takeaway
Act on the A1c above goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

## Why this answer is correct
Switch lisinopril to losartan 50 mg daily.
• The new cough is most likely ACE-inhibitor cough; an ARB keeps RAAS blockade in diabetes without the cough.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Amlodipine 5 mg daily / Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily / Diltiazem 120 mg daily**: They do not replace RAAS blockade in diabetes.
## Key takeaway
ACE-inhibitor cough: switch to an ARB.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 10)

newKeyText: Start a combination inhaler with an anticholinergic.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Start a LAMA/LABA combination inhaler.
• GOLD 2025 recommends LAMA/LABA for symptomatic COPD; ICS/LABA is not recommended in COPD, and ICS is added only with frequent exacerbations and high eosinophils.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Continue albuterol as needed**: SABA alone is insufficient for moderate symptomatic COPD.
• **Switch to a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) only**: LABA monotherapy is less effective than LAMA/LABA.
• **Initiate a leukotriene receptor antagonist**: Leukotriene antagonists have no role in COPD.
## Key takeaway
COPD maintenance: LAMA/LABA, not ICS/LABA.
(Guideline: GOLD 2025)

## Why this answer is correct
An SGLT2 inhibitor is the best weight-favorable alternative.
• SGLT2 inhibitors lower A1c and cause modest weight loss without hypoglycemia (ADA SOC 2026), meeting his concern about weight gain.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Insulin glargine**: Insulin causes weight gain.
• **Thiazolidinedione**: Thiazolidinediones cause weight gain and edema.
• **Sulfonylurea**: Sulfonylureas cause weight gain and hypoglycemia.
## Key takeaway
Weight-favorable options: GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 9)

currentKeyText: Interest in starting a new medication
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
The A1c of 7.8% needs follow-up.
• An A1c above the usual <7% goal supports adding an agent, ideally a weight-favorable one (ADA SOC 2026).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Interest in starting a new medication / Concern about weight gain**: Her wishes guide drug choice but are not clinical findings.
• **No significant renal impairment**: Normal renal function is reassuring.
## Key takeaway
Act on the A1c above goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

## Why this answer is correct
Add a GLP-1 receptor agonist.
• With A1c 9.2% on maximal metformin, ADA SOC 2026 recommends adding a high-efficacy agent such as a GLP-1 RA before insulin unless A1c exceeds 10% or catabolic symptoms are present.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase metformin to 2000 mg daily**: He already takes metformin 2,000 mg/day.
• **Add a DPP-4 inhibitor**: DPP-4 inhibitors have modest efficacy.
• **Start insulin therapy**: Insulin is generally reserved for A1c above 10% or symptoms.
## Key takeaway
A1c well above goal on metformin: add a GLP-1 RA.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 9)

## Why this answer is correct
An SGLT2 inhibitor such as canagliflozin is the best alternative.
• KDIGO 2022 recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor for T2D with eGFR 20 or higher for kidney and CV protection; metformin labeling does not recommend starting metformin at eGFR 30-45.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Insulin glargine (Lantus)**: Insulin is not needed first.
• **DPP-4 inhibitor (sitagliptin)**: Sitagliptin requires dose reduction and lacks kidney benefit.
• **GLP-1 receptor agonist (liraglutide)**: Liraglutide is reasonable but lacks the kidney-outcome recommendation of SGLT2 inhibitors in CKD.
## Key takeaway
T2D with CKD: SGLT2 inhibitor.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD; ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 11)

currentKeyText: Administer with food to minimize gastrointestinal upset.
newKeyText: Administer 10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours as needed.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Give 10 mg/kg (200 mg) every 6-8 hours as needed.
• Pediatric ibuprofen is 5-10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours, maximum 40 mg/kg/day; for 20 kg that is 200 mg per dose.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Do not exceed 400 mg per dose**: 400 mg is an adult-size dose and double his weight-based dose.
• **Use ibuprofen only if the fever exceeds 101°F**: Treat discomfort, not a specific temperature.
• **Administer with food to minimize gastrointestinal upset**: Food is optional.
## Key takeaway
Pediatric ibuprofen: 10 mg/kg every 6-8 hours.
(Guideline: Pediatric ibuprofen labeling; AAP fever guidance)

## Why this answer is correct
Canagliflozin (an SGLT2 inhibitor) is the best choice.
• KDIGO 2022 recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor for T2D with CKD (eGFR 20 or higher) for kidney and CV protection; canagliflozin is limited to 100 mg at eGFR below 60.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Sitagliptin**: Sitagliptin needs dose reduction (50 mg) at eGFR 30-44 and has no kidney benefit.
• **Glyburide**: Glyburide causes prolonged hypoglycemia in CKD.
• **Insulin glargine**: Insulin is not needed.
## Key takeaway
T2D with CKD: SGLT2 inhibitor.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD)

## Why this answer is correct
The A1c of 9.2% needs follow-up.
• An A1c of 9.2% on metformin requires intensification (ADA SOC 2026); GI effects can be managed with extended-release metformin.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Gastrointestinal side effects**: GI effects are manageable and secondary.
• **Stable renal function**: Stable renal function is reassuring.
• **Adherence to medication regimen**: Adherence is good.
## Key takeaway
Act on the A1c above goal.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 6)

## Why this answer is correct
The LDL of 160 mg/dL needs follow-up.
• An LDL of 160 on a statin shows inadequate response; assess adherence and intensify (2018 ACC/AHA).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Current atorvastatin dosage**: The dose is not given and is not itself a finding.
• **Patient's age**: Age is not a finding.
• **No other medications**: No other medications is not a concern.
## Key takeaway
Follow up an LDL above goal on statin therapy.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

currentKeyText: I should take two puffs of the inhaler every day.
newKeyText: I should not use the inhaler if I feel fine.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
The belief that he should skip the inhaler when feeling fine needs correction.
• Tiotropium is a once-daily maintenance bronchodilator that must be used every day regardless of symptoms (GOLD 2025).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **I should take two puffs of the inhaler every day**: Daily inhalation of the dose is correct.
• **I need to rinse my mouth after using the inhaler**: Rinsing is harmless (required for ICS, not LAMA).
• **I should store the inhaler in a cool, dry place**: Storage in a cool, dry place is correct.
## Key takeaway
Maintenance inhalers are used daily even when feeling well.
(Guideline: Tiotropium (Spiriva HandiHaler) labeling; GOLD 2025)

## Why this answer is correct
The fasting glucose of 220 mg/dL needs follow-up.
• A fasting glucose of 220 on basal insulin means the glargine dose needs titration (e.g., raise 2 units every 3 days to target), while watching for hypoglycemia given her history.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Recent weight gain / Increased thirst / Frequent urination**: Weight gain, thirst and urination are not described.
## Key takeaway
Titrate basal insulin to fasting glucose.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 9)

newKeyText: CPK levels if muscle pain occurs.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Check CK if muscle pain occurs.
• The guideline does not recommend routine CK or liver monitoring; CK is checked in patients with muscle symptoms, which addresses his concern.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Liver function tests every 6 months**: Routine LFTs are not recommended after a normal baseline.
• **Creatinine levels every 3 months**: Creatinine every 3 months is not needed.
• **Lipid panel every 3 months**: Lipids are checked 4-12 weeks after starting, then every 3-12 months.
## Key takeaway
Statin monitoring: CK only with symptoms; no routine LFTs.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
His increased bruising and bleeding need follow-up.
• New bruising and bleeding on clopidogrel need evaluation for bleeding risk, interacting drugs and, rarely, TTP.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Elevated liver enzymes / Decreased platelet count / Increased blood pressure**: No liver, platelet or BP results are given.
## Key takeaway
Evaluate new bleeding in antiplatelet users.
(Guideline: Clopidogrel labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
Rechallenge with a different statin such as rosuvastatin.
• After statin-associated muscle symptoms resolve, the guideline advises rechallenging with a different statin or lower dose; ezetimibe is added only if statins are not tolerated.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Simvastatin**: Simvastatin carries a higher myopathy risk.
• **Ezetimibe**: Ezetimibe is for confirmed intolerance.
• **Niacin**: Niacin has no outcome benefit.
## Key takeaway
Statin muscle symptoms: rechallenge with another statin first.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

currentKeyText: Continue metformin at the same dose and monitor renal function.
newKeyText: Reduce the metformin dose to 500 mg twice daily.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Reduce metformin to 500 mg twice daily and retitrate slowly.
• GI effects are dose-related; lowering the dose and titrating up slowly (or switching to extended-release) improves tolerance. eGFR 55 needs no renal adjustment.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Continue metformin at the same dose and monitor renal function**: Continuing the same dose ignores his GI effects.
• **Discontinue metformin and switch to glipizide**: A sulfonylurea adds hypoglycemia risk in an older adult.
• **Increase the metformin dose to 1500 mg twice daily**: 3,000 mg/day exceeds the usual 2,000-2,550 mg maximum and worsens GI effects.
## Key takeaway
Metformin GI upset: lower the dose, titrate slowly, or use ER.
(Guideline: Metformin labeling; ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 9)

## Why this answer is correct
Add memantine.
• For moderate-to-severe Alzheimer disease progressing on a cholinesterase inhibitor, adding memantine is recommended (titrate from 5 mg daily to 10 mg twice daily).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Rivastigmine 1.5 mg twice daily / Galantamine 8 mg twice daily**: Switching to another cholinesterase inhibitor adds little.
• **Donepezil 5 mg daily**: Lowering donepezil reduces efficacy.
## Key takeaway
Progression on donepezil: add memantine.
(Guideline: APA 2007 dementia guideline; AAN; memantine labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
Continue atorvastatin.
• After coronary stenting, a high-intensity statin such as atorvastatin is indicated; the theoretical CYP3A4 interaction with clopidogrel is not clinically significant, so no switch is needed.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Simvastatin**: Simvastatin is less potent and has more interactions.
• **Rosuvastatin**: Rosuvastatin is an option but switching offers no advantage.
• **Pravastatin**: Pravastatin is low-to-moderate intensity.
## Key takeaway
Post-PCI: keep the high-intensity statin; atorvastatin with clopidogrel is fine.
(Guideline: 2023 ACC/AHA chronic coronary disease guideline; 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol)

## Why this answer is correct
Step up by increasing the fluticasone/salmeterol dose.
• Albuterol use 4 times a week with night symptoms means uncontrolled asthma; for a child on low-dose ICS-LABA, GINA steps up to medium-dose ICS-LABA after checking technique and adherence.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add montelukast**: Montelukast is a less effective add-on with a boxed neuropsychiatric warning.
• **Switch to a different inhaled corticosteroid**: Switching ICS without raising the dose does not step up.
• **Add a short-acting beta-agonist**: He already has a SABA.
## Key takeaway
Uncontrolled on ICS-LABA: check technique, then step up.
(Guideline: GINA 2024/2025 (children 6-11))

## Why this answer is correct
Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily.
• Lisinopril needs a lower starting dose only at CrCl 30 or below; at CrCl 45 the usual dose is appropriate and ACE inhibition is preferred in diabetes.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Lisinopril 10 mg daily**: A dose reduction is not required at CrCl 45.
• **Amlodipine 5 mg daily / Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily**: Amlodipine or HCTZ would replace the preferred RAAS blocker.
## Key takeaway
Lisinopril: adjust only at CrCl 30 or below.
(Guideline: Lisinopril labeling; ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 10)

## Why this answer is correct
Hemoglobin is the most important parameter after surgery.
• After major orthopedic surgery on apixaban, bleeding is the main risk; hemoglobin/CBC monitoring detects it.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **INR**: INR does not measure apixaban effect.
• **eGFR**: EGFR 65 is stable.
• **Liver function tests**: Liver tests are not the priority.
## Key takeaway
Post-op on a DOAC: watch hemoglobin for bleeding.
(Guideline: Apixaban labeling; CHEST 2022 perioperative guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
Increase atorvastatin to 80 mg daily.
• LDL remains 160 on a moderate dose; the guideline maximizes statin intensity before adding a non-statin.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add ezetimibe 10 mg daily**: Ezetimibe is added after maximal tolerated statin.
• **Switch to simvastatin 40 mg daily**: Simvastatin 40 is less potent.
• **Add niacin 500 mg daily**: Niacin has no outcome benefit.
## Key takeaway
Maximize the statin before adding a non-statin.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
Add an SGLT2 inhibitor.
• For T2D with heart failure and CKD, SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF hospitalization and kidney progression (ADA SOC 2026; KDIGO 2022).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **DPP-4 inhibitor**: DPP-4 inhibitors lack HF/kidney benefit.
• **GLP-1 receptor agonist**: GLP-1 RAs are second choice for HF/CKD.
• **Thiazolidinedione**: Thiazolidinediones worsen HF.
## Key takeaway
T2D with HF or CKD: SGLT2 inhibitor.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 9/10/11; KDIGO 2022)

## Why this answer is correct
Rechallenge with a different statin such as rosuvastatin.
• After statin-associated muscle symptoms resolve, the guideline advises rechallenging with a different statin or lower dose; ezetimibe is used if statins are not tolerated.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Ezetimibe**: Ezetimibe is for confirmed statin intolerance.
• **Niacin**: Niacin has no outcome benefit.
• **Fenofibrate**: Fenofibrate targets triglycerides.
## Key takeaway
Statin muscle symptoms: rechallenge with another statin first.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
Continue metformin 1,000 mg twice daily.
• At eGFR 45 metformin may continue at standard dose with eGFR checks every 3-6 months (KDIGO 2022); reduce only below 45.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Sitagliptin 100 mg daily**: Sitagliptin must be reduced to 50 mg at eGFR 30-44.
• **Glipizide 5 mg daily**: Glipizide adds hypoglycemia risk.
• **Insulin glargine 10 units at bedtime**: Insulin is not needed.
## Key takeaway
Metformin continues at eGFR 45.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD; ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 11)

## Why this answer is correct
Metformin 500 mg twice daily is appropriate.
• At eGFR 45, a cautious start of 500 mg twice daily with slow titration fits labeling and KDIGO 2022 (maximum 1,000 mg/day if eGFR falls to 30-44).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **850 mg BID**: 1,700 mg/day is too aggressive a start.
• **1000 mg daily**: 1,000 mg IR once daily is not the usual regimen and worsens GI effects.
• **250 mg BID**: 250 mg twice daily is subtherapeutic.
## Key takeaway
Metformin near eGFR 45: start low (500 mg BID).
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD; metformin labeling)

currentKeyText: Continue metformin as it is safe in pregnancy.
newKeyText: Switch to insulin for better glycemic control.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Switch to insulin.
• Insulin is the preferred agent for type 2 diabetes in pregnancy; metformin crosses the placenta and alone often cannot reach pregnancy targets (A1c <6-6.5%).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Continue metformin as it is safe in pregnancy**: Metformin is not the preferred agent.
• **Discontinue all diabetes medications during pregnancy**: Stopping therapy causes harmful hyperglycemia.
• **Start glyburide instead of metformin**: Glyburide crosses the placenta and is not recommended.
## Key takeaway
Diabetes in pregnancy: insulin preferred.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026 Sec. 15)

## Why this answer is correct
No adjustment: 1,000 mg twice daily is appropriate.
• Standard metformin dosing continues at eGFR 45 or higher (KDIGO 2022); CrCl 50 needs no change.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **1000 mg once daily / 500 mg twice daily**: Reductions to 1,000 mg/day are for eGFR 30-44.
• **1500 mg once daily**: 1,500 mg once daily is not a standard IR regimen.
## Key takeaway
Metformin: no dose change at eGFR 45 or higher.
(Guideline: KDIGO 2022 Diabetes in CKD; metformin labeling)

## Why this answer is correct
The lipid panel is the key monitoring parameter.
• The guideline checks lipids 4-12 weeks after a statin change and then every 3-12 months; routine liver and CK monitoring is not recommended.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Liver function tests every 6 weeks**: Routine LFTs are not recommended after a normal baseline.
• **Creatine kinase levels every 3 months**: CK is checked only with muscle symptoms.
• **Blood glucose levels every 3 months**: Glucose every 3 months is not required.
## Key takeaway
After a statin change, monitor lipids; no routine LFTs or CK.
(Guideline: 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline)
